scope: UK educational teaching surface with primary-source market/index definitions. Direct access allowed; guided entry remains Money Decision INVESTING_READINESS.

nodes.label: Investing
nodes.definition: Putting money into assets with the aim of receiving a return over time. Values can rise or fall. There is no risk-free investment.
nodes.firstPrinciple: This page teaches the idea of investing. It does not say investing is suitable for you.

nodes.label: Review debt
nodes.definition: Short-term debt should generally be prioritised before investing. Do not use credit to invest.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Debt review is an ordering rule, not a list of which debt to pay first.

nodes.label: Emergency savings
nodes.definition: Keep accessible emergency savings before committing money to investments.
nodes.firstPrinciple: This page explains that a buffer comes before investing education. It does not set your personal buffer size.

nodes.label: Workplace pension
nodes.pageSection: Start with your financial foundations; UK accounts and pensions
nodes.definition: If you are employed, consider your workplace pension as part of your foundations. Schemes often receive employer contributions and invest for retirement. Check your own scheme rules.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Generic contribution examples are not your contribution recommendation.

nodes.label: Time horizon
nodes.definition: Money needed soon is different from long-term money. MoneyHelper discusses investing as longer-term, including goals more than five years away. The FCA notes that for a fairly short timeframe, perhaps up to three years, savings may be more appropriate to explore.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Three years and five years are educational guideposts, not a personal suitability test.

nodes.label: Shares, bonds and cash
nodes.definition: MoneyHelper groups common investment types by characteristic. Shares are a stake in a company. Bonds are IOUs for lending to a company or government. Cash in a bank or building society account is listed alongside those types, but it is saving, not investing.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Naming types is not choosing a mix. Property and REITs stay out of this node.

nodes.label: Pooled funds
nodes.definition: Collective funds pool money and typically invest in a broad basket of shares or bonds. That pooling is one way diversification shows up in practice. Directly buying a small number of shares is more concentrated.
nodes.firstPrinciple: A fund is a vehicle. This page does not name a fund, platform, or wrapper-as-product.

nodes.label: Tracker funds
nodes.definition: Active funds try to beat a market index; outperformance is not guaranteed and they can do worse. Tracker funds take a passive approach and aim to match an index. Tracker management charges are typically lower. The FCA uses the UK FTSE 100 as an example of a market index, not as a product to buy.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Explain matching versus beating an index. Do not say start with a tracker, name an ETF, or treat the S&P 500 as the default portfolio.

nodes.label: Risk
nodes.definition: Investment values can fall as well as rise. Understand how much loss you could tolerate while still meeting your goals.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Naming risk is not a regulated risk-profile or a recommendation to take risk.

nodes.label: Diversification
nodes.definition: Spreading exposure across different assets and markets can reduce reliance on any single investment. It cannot remove investment risk. Pooled funds are one educational example of that spreading.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Diversification is a concept, not an asset-allocation recipe.

nodes.label: Costs
nodes.definition: Investment and service-provider fees reduce the returns you keep. Upfront and ongoing costs are part of comparing options. Tracker charges are typically lower than active-fund charges; that is a cost fact, not a buy instruction.
nodes.firstPrinciple: This page does not quantify a '1% fee costs hundreds of thousands' claim.

nodes.label: Individual Savings Account
nodes.definition: ISAs can hold cash or eligible investments and provide tax advantages. A Stocks and Shares ISA is a tax wrapper, not a guarantee that holdings will make money.
nodes.firstPrinciple: A wrapper changes tax treatment. It does not remove investment risk or name a provider.

nodes.label: Promised high or guaranteed returns
nodes.definition: Be cautious of promotions that promise very high or guaranteed returns or present investing as a quick way to get rich. Understand the risks before committing money.
nodes.firstPrinciple: This is a caution, not a claim that any promotion is a scam.

nodes.label: US, UK, Europe and Asia
nodes.pageSection: Markets: US, UK, Europe and Asia
nodes.definition: Market groupings describe coverage, not a ranking. Europe, EU and eurozone differ; Asia contains distinct markets.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Do not recommend a region or equate an index with the whole economy.

nodes.label: Market indices
nodes.definition: An index measures a defined set of securities. It is a benchmark, not a fund.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Named benchmarks are examples, not products to buy.

nodes.label: World index coverage
nodes.definition: MSCI World covers developed markets including US equities; MSCI ACWI covers developed and emerging markets. Neither means every stock or every asset.
nodes.firstPrinciple: No fixed weights, rankings, or portfolio allocation.

nodes.label: S&P 500
nodes.definition: A benchmark of large US companies, not the whole world or the entire US stock market.
nodes.firstPrinciple: Explain coverage only. No recommendation to buy an S&P 500 fund.

nodes.label: Exchange-traded funds
nodes.definition: Fund shares traded on an exchange. ETFs may track an index or use active management. Structure alone does not imply broad diversification or safety.
nodes.firstPrinciple: No named fund, ticker, provider recommendation, or foreign tax/protection claim.
